```lua
local part = script.Parent
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if plr then
        plr.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 10
        part:Destroy()
    end
end)
```
Explain the cause and give a fix.
answer_key: Touched fires repeatedly/multiple times in quick succession (once per touching body part / physics contact), so the handler runs several times
Fix: add a debounce/cooldown or 'already collected' flag checked and set at the top of the handler before awarding (per-part flag, or per-player timestamp table)
Award on the server only; the flag is set synchronously before any yield so re-entrant events cannot double-grant

Touched fires many times: once for every body part (feet, legs, HumanoidRootPart) and repeatedly while they overlap. Destroy only takes effect after the current events, so several handlers run before the part is gone, and each one adds 10. Fix it with a server-side debounce or claimed flag that is set before granting:
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local claimed = false
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
  if claimed then return end
  local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
  if not plr then return end
  local coins = plr:FindFirstChild('leaderstats') and plr.leaderstats:FindFirstChild('Coins')
  if not coins then return end
  claimed = true
  coins.Value += 10
  part:Destroy()
end)
```

```lua
  if not plr then return end
```

```lua
local MPS = game:GetService('MarketplaceService')
MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    local ok = pcall(function()
        store:SetAsync(plr.UserId, (store:GetAsync(plr.UserId) or 0) + 100)
    end)
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
List the bugs and the corrected behavior.
answer_key: Returns PurchaseGranted unconditionally: if the DataStore call fails (ok == false) or the player has left (plr is nil), it must return NotProcessedYet so the receipt is retried
Not idempotent: receipts can be re-delivered, so record info.PurchaseId and skip the grant if already processed (ideally inside one UpdateAsync)
Uses non-atomic Get+Set instead of UpdateAsync, and plr is not nil-checked (errors when the player left)

A hitscan gun uses this and almost never registers hits, even point-blank:
```lua
local dir = (target - origin).Unit
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir)
if r then print(r.Instance) end
```
What is wrong and how do you fix it?
answer_key: The direction vector's magnitude is the ray length; a unit vector gives a 1-stud ray
Fix: scale the direction by the range (dir * range) or pass (target - origin) unnormalized; max length is 15,000 studs
Check the result for nil before using it (no hit returns nil)

responses.R1:
workspace:Raycast's direction is the full ray vector - its length is the ray distance. A .Unit vector is 1 stud long, so the ray stops after 1 stud. Fix: use the displacement or unit * range, and exclude the shooter:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 500  -- or (target - origin)
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
responses.R2:
workspace:Raycast's second argument is the ray's direction including its length. A .Unit vector is only 1 stud long, so it almost never reaches the target. The ray can also hit the shooter's own character. Fix:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 500 -- max range
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Or use (target - origin) directly to cast exactly to the target.
responses.R3:
workspace:Raycast(origin, direction) uses the length of the direction vector as the ray's distance. .Unit gives length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud. It also starts inside the shooter's own character, which it may hit. Fix: give the direction a real length and exclude the shooter.
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 300 -- max range
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
(Or use (target - origin) directly to reach exactly the target, clamped to max range.) Do hit validation on the server.

workspace:Raycast's second argument is a direction vector whose length is the ray length. `.Unit` makes it 1 stud long, so the ray stops 1 stud from the origin. It also likely hits the shooter's own character/tool, since there's no RaycastParams filter.
Fix:
```lua

params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}

local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX_RANGE
```

prompt: A shop UI must (a) let the player buy a sword with in-game coins and (b) update the on-screen coin counter afterward. prompt: A map has 400 doors, 150 pickups and 60 turrets. Compare giving every instance its own Script with a tag-driven architecture, and describe the recommended structure including how newly spawned or streamed-in instances are handled.
answer_key: Use CollectionService tags (e.g. 'Door', 'Pickup', 'Turret') with one controller script/ModuleScript per behavior instead of hundreds of duplicated scripts
Initialize with GetTagged for existing instances plus GetInstanceAddedSignal for later ones, and GetInstanceRemovedSignal for cleanup of connections/state
Benefits: single code path, easier updates, works with cloned/streamed instances; per-instance config via attributes

responses.R1: Per-instance Scripts: 610 copies of near-identical code, each with its own thread and connections; hard to update (edit every copy, drift), more memory and startup cost, and awkward with spawning/streaming. Tag-driven: tag instances (Door, Pickup, Turret) with CollectionService; one server Script/module per tag uses GetTagged + GetInstanceAddedSignal to bind behaviour and GetInstanceRemovedSignal to clean up (per-instance state/connections in a table keyed by instance, disconnected on removal); per-instance config via Attributes. Newly spawned instances bind automatically when a tagged template is cloned; on clients with StreamingEnabled, streamed-in instances fire InstanceAdded and streamed-out fire InstanceRemoved, so client visuals bind/unbind correctly. Turrets can share one Heartbeat loop over the tracked set instead of one loop each.
responses.R2: Giving 610 instances their own Script means 610 copies of code. It's hard to update or fix (copies drift), uses more memory and startup work and more threads and connections, makes cleanup inconsistent, and copies are easy to miss or duplicate. A tag-driven architecture tags instances ('Door', 'Pickup', 'Turret') with CollectionService. One server Script/module per tag (a service) runs setup and teardown for every tagged instance and keeps per-instance state in a table keyed by instance. Use config from attributes (for example Damage or Range), and drive turrets from one central loop/Heartbeat with a budget instead of 60 loops. Structure: ServerScriptService/Services/DoorService, PickupService, TurretService, plus client-side tag modules for visuals. Handling new instances: connect GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag) and also iterate GetTagged(tag) for existing ones, and make setup idempotent. Clean up connections and state on GetInstanceRemovedSignal (which also fires on Destroy or, on clients, streaming out). Spawned clones keep their tags. With StreamingEnabled, client code only reacts to added/removed, so streamed-in doors work automatically, and server logic stays authoritative.
responses.R3: Per-instance Scripts (610 copies) are hard to maintain (fixing a bug means editing every copy), cost memory and startup time, duplicate connections and state, and break on streamed/spawned instances. Recommended: tag instances with CollectionService (Door, Pickup, Turret) and have one server Script/module per behaviour (plus client modules for visuals) that binds to GetTagged and GetInstanceAddedSignal, and cleans up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal (disconnect connections, a per-instance state/Janitor table). Configuration via Attributes on each instance. Newly spawned instances get the tag (e.g. from templates) and are picked up by the added signal; on the client, streamed-in instances fire the added signal when they arrive and the removed signal when streamed out, so clients handle streaming naturally. Turrets can share one Heartbeat loop over a set instead of 60 loops.
responses.R4:
Per-instance Scripts (610 copies): each Script is a separate VM thread/ connections set, duplicated code that must be edited in 610 places, harder memory/perf, copies drift, poor with streaming (scripts in streamed parts on client), and spawned clones bring their own scripts.
Tag-driven: tag instances with CollectionService ("Door", "Pickup", "Turret"), one server Script (or module per type) per tag: iterate CollectionService:GetTagged(tag) for existing instances, connect GetInstanceAddedSignal(tag) for newly spawned/cloned or streamed-in instances, and GetInstanceRemovedSignal(tag) to disconnect/clean up (Janitor/Trove per instance). Structure: ServerScriptService/Systems/DoorSystem, PickupSystem, TurretSystem (ModuleScripts started by one bootstrap), shared config in ReplicatedStorage.

prompt: You are building a racing game with drivable cars. Decide who should have network ownership of the car, what the security risk is, and what the server must still validate.
answer_key: The driver's client should own the car for responsive physics (SetNetworkOwner on the server when seated; release to automatic when empty); the server always owns anchored parts
Client ownership means Roblox cannot verify the physics: exploiters can teleport parts or move them through walls, and Touched events on owned parts can be fired by that client
Server must validate critical outcomes (checkpoints, lap times, speed/position plausibility, damage); use SetNetworkOwner(nil) for gameplay-critical parts
Use ownership changes sparingly because they can cause jitter

responses.R1: Give network ownership of the car to the driver: in the VehicleSeat's Occupant change, call SetNetworkOwner(driverPlayer) on the chassis assembly. Return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or set auto ownership when they exit. That gives responsive, lag-free driving, while server ownership would feel laggy. The risk: the owning client fully controls that assembly's physics, so an exploiter can teleport it, speed-hack, fly, fling other players, or skip checkpoints, and the server just accepts the replicated positions. The server must still validate: speed and acceleration plausibility (distance per time against the car's max speed), teleport jumps, position bounds or noclip through walls, and checkpoint order with timing (sequential gates, minimum lap time). Lap counts, finish and race results, and rewards are decided on the server, never reported by the client. Collisions or damage to others should be sanity-checked. On violation, reset the car or take ownership back. Also make sure only the seated driver owns it, and clear ownership on exit or death.

This gives responsive, lag-free physics for the driver. When they exit, return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) and keep parked or empty cars server-owned or anchored. The risk is that the owning client simulates the physics and the server accepts it, so an exploiter can teleport the car, speed-hack, fly, noclip, fling other players, or fake lap and checkpoint progress. The server must still validate speed and acceleration (max per car type, with tolerance), the position delta per tick and teleports, staying on the track or ground, checkpoint order and timing (lap times above the minimum possible), and collisions or flings on others. It should handle all lap, finish, reward and damage logic, and use strike counts and reset rather than instant kicks. For competitive racing, consider Server Authority mode (2026), which uses server simulation with client prediction instead of client ownership.
responses.R3: Give the driver network ownership of the car (vehicle:SetNetworkOwner(driver) on the server when they sit, and back to the server or nil on exit) for smooth, responsive physics without input latency. Server ownership feels laggy. Risk: the owner's client simulates the car, so an exploiter can set any position or velocity: teleporting, speed hacks, flying, ramming others. The server must still validate: speed/position deltas against the car's max speed and acceleration (sanity checks per tick, with rubber-banding or a reset on violation), checkpoint order and lap times done server-side (Touched or region checks on the server, never client-reported), seat occupancy and who may drive, collision damage and race results. Don't trust remotes like 'I finished'. Server Authority mode (2026) is an alternative for fully server-authoritative prediction.

Ownership: give the driver network ownership of the car (VehicleSeat occupant -> server calls part:SetNetworkOwner(driverPlayer) on the chassis when they sit; SetNetworkOwner(nil) or auto when they leave). prompt: A shooter sends each player's aim direction and position to the server 30 times per second via a RemoteEvent, causing bandwidth and queue pressure. Recommend a better transport and describe its constraints and how to handle them.

Payloads over 1,000 bytes may be dropped, so keep messages small

Handling: keep payloads tiny (a few numbers - e.g. compressed direction/position, buffer or quantized values, no instances/tables); include a sequence number or timestamp and ignore older packets (latest-wins); treat each packet as full current state, not a delta, so drops don't matter; interpolate on receivers; reduce rate (e.g. 10-20 Hz) or send only when aim changes significantly; validate on the server (type, NaN/inf, rate per player, position plausibility vs. server character). Handle: send compact data (numbers, quantize/compress the direction, e.g. buffer or Vector3int16), include a sequence number or timestamp and ignore older packets, reduce frequency (send only on change/10-20 Hz) and interpolate on receivers, keep important one-off events (shots, hits) on a reliable RemoteEvent, and validate/rate-limit on the server. Handling: send the latest full state each time rather than deltas, include a sequence number or timestamp, and discard stale or out-of-order packets on the receiver. Interpolate or extrapolate on observers. Reduce the rate (10-20 Hz) and only send on meaningful change. Keep important one-time events (fire, hit, reload) on a reliable RemoteEvent. Validate on the server and rate-limit. prompt: Server frame time spikes because 200 NPCs each do several raycasts and path scoring every Heartbeat on the main thread. How would you use Parallel Luau for this, and what limitations must you design around?
answer_key: Split NPC logic across multiple Actors (scripts under one Actor run serially, so parallelism needs several Actors)
Use task.desynchronize() (or ConnectParallel) for the heavy read/compute work such as raycasts, then task.synchronize() before modifying the data model
Most property writes/functions are unsafe in parallel so results are applied in a serial phase; require() cannot be called in a desynchronized phase
Use SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel or SharedTable for cross-Actor data; avoid long unyielding computations

responses.R1:
Parallel Luau: put the NPC logic in scripts under Actor instances (e.g. split 200 NPCs across N Actors, ~cores x 2-4, or one Actor per NPC group). Each Actor's script connects RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) and does the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is safe in parallel), path scoring, target selection, math. Then task.synchronize() (or a later serial phase) to apply results: move humanoids, set properties, fire remotes, damage. Communicate via Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage(Parallel) or SharedTable.
Limits: in the parallel phase you can't write most instance properties or call non-thread-safe APIs (writes only to instances in your own Actor's subtree for some; check thread-safety tags); no yielding inside desynchronized code; modules required in each Actor are separate copies (no shared Lua state; use SharedTable for shared data); data passed via messages is copied; overhead of sync/desync per frame. Also reduce work: stagger NPC updates across frames, LOD by distance, cache paths (ComputeAsync not every frame).
responses.R2: Split the NPCs into Actors: put each group of NPCs (for example 10-25 per Actor) under an Actor instance with its own Script, or move the NPC scripts under Actors. In each, connect RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), distance and path scoring, target selection. Then call task.synchronize() to apply the results in serial: set Humanoid:MoveTo, CFrames and properties, fire events. Limitations: in the parallel phase you can only read the DataModel. Writes to most properties, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs (PathfindingService:ComputeAsync etc.) are disallowed. Do the writes after synchronize. Actors don't share Lua state: communicate via Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage, attributes, or SharedTable. Each Actor has its own VM, so module requires are duplicated and there's memory overhead. Per-thread overhead means too many tiny actors is slow. Also throttle the work: stagger NPCs over frames, use lower tick rates for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
responses.R3:
Split NPCs across several Actors (e.g. 8-16 Actor instances, each with a Script handling a subset of NPC ids; not one Actor and not 200). In each worker, run the expensive read-only work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(fn) (or Actor:BindToMessageParallel), do raycasts (workspace:Raycast works in parallel), distance checks and path scoring, store results locally, then task.synchronize() and apply results (set CFrames, Humanoid:MoveTo, fire events) in serial. Throttle: not every NPC every frame.
Limitations:
- In the parallel phase you can't create/destroy/reparent instances or write most properties (non-thread-safe members error "not safe in parallel"); reads and spatial queries are fine.
- Each Actor is its own Luau VM: module state isn't shared; require modules in serial at load; communicate via Actor:SendMessage (args copied) or SharedTable (SharedTableRegistry; atomic updates, no functions/Instance keys).
- Scripts must be descendants of the Actor; instances modified should be under that Actor.
- Overhead of sync/messaging can exceed gains for small work; measure with the MicroProfiler. Pathfinding (PathfindingService) yields and isn't parallel-safe - compute paths in serial/occasionally.
responses.R4: Put NPCs under many Actors (one per NPC or per group), each with a Script that runs the heavy work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize) to do raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe) and path scoring, keep results in locals, then task.synchronize() before writing Instance properties (movement, damage, attributes). Limitations: no Instance writes or most mutating APIs in the parallel phase (reads only); each Actor has its own Lua VM, so module state isn't shared - use SharedTable (atomic ops like SharedTable.increment) or Actor messaging (SendMessage / BindToMessageParallel); scripts must be descendants of the Actor; sync/desync switches cost time, so batch work; some APIs (e.g. PathfindingService ComputeAsync) aren't parallel-safe; also stagger work across frames instead of every NPC every Heartbeat. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
responses.R5: Split NPCs across several Actors (e.g. 8-16, each owning a batch of NPC scripts/models, or a pooled worker script under each Actor). In each actor, run the work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize) to do raycasts, distance checks and path scoring (reads and spatial queries are allowed in parallel); collect results; then task.synchronize() to apply writes (move to, CFrame/property changes, firing events). Limitations: most instance property writes and many APIs are unsafe in parallel and require synchronize; scripts can only modify instances under their own Actor; data between actors is copied (Actor:SendMessage, SharedTable for shared state); module state isn't shared between actors (each requires its own copy); overhead of sync points, so batch per frame; pathfinding ComputeAsync yields (do it serially/staggered); always profile with the MicroProfiler. Also stagger updates over frames and reduce frequency for distant NPCs.
responses.R6: Split the NPCs across several Actors (for example 8-16 Actors with about 12-25 NPCs each, or one script per Actor driving a batch), not one Actor, which gives no speed-up. In each Actor, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run raycasts and path scoring in parallel. workspace:Raycast and reading properties are allowed in parallel. Then call task.synchronize() (or queue the results) to apply the writes, like moving NPCs, setting properties, Humanoid:MoveTo and firing remotes, in the serial phase. Limitations: most instance property writes, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs aren't allowed while desynchronized. Each Actor has its own Luau VM, so module state isn't shared. Communicate through Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage (arguments are copied, so send ids, not big tables) or SharedTable (for shared data, with atomic update/increment). Require modules at load time. Parallel results only apply at the sync point (a one-frame delay). Also cut the work: spread NPC updates over several frames, lower the update rate for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile in the MicroProfiler Threads view first.
responses.R7: Split the NPCs across several Actors (for example 8-16 Actors, each with a script handling a group of NPCs, or one Actor per NPC model). In each Actor, use RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is safe in parallel), path scoring and target selection. Then call task.synchronize() and apply the results (CFrame, Humanoid:MoveTo, attribute writes) in the serial phase. Limitations: most instance property writes and many APIs are not allowed in the parallel phase (they error); Actors don't share Lua state, so communicate through Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel (arguments are copied) or SharedTable (watch for races and use atomic update/increment). There's no require inside the parallel phase, scripts must be descendants of an Actor, and the overhead means tiny tasks gain nothing. Also reduce the work: run AI at about 10 Hz, stagger the NPCs, and gate by distance. Profile with the MicroProfiler first.

prompt: An open-world game has long join times and high client memory on mobile. StreamingEnabled is off. What do you change in Workspace, which defaults/radii are sensible, and what do you do to scripts that assumed everything is loaded?
answer_key: Turn StreamingEnabled on (default for new places); keep default StreamingMinRadius 64 and StreamingTargetRadius 1024 unless profiling says otherwise (target larger than min)
Prefer ModelStreamingBehavior Improved and Opportunistic StreamOutBehavior; use Atomic for models that must arrive whole, Persistent only sparingly
Update client scripts to use WaitForChild/PersistentLoaded and tolerate parts streaming in/out, or move logic to the server; raycasts can miss unstreamed parts

responses.R1: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Sensible settings: StreamingMinRadius about 64-128 studs, StreamingTargetRadius about 256-1024 (the default is 64 min / 1024 target; lower it for mobile or dense maps). StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic (to free memory on low-end devices), StreamingIntegrityMode = MinimumRadiusPause (or PauseOutsideLoadedArea) so players don't fall into unloaded areas. Use Model.ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must arrive whole, Persistent only for a few always-needed models (spawn, key landmarks), PersistentPerPlayer where needed. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant silhouettes. Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleports or cutscenes. Scripts: client code can't assume parts exist. Replace direct indexing with WaitForChild (with timeouts), use CollectionService tag signals or ChildAdded to hook objects as they stream in, and clean up when they stream out (instances may be destroyed and re-created). Keep authoritative logic on the server, which has everything. Don't hold references to far-away parts, and avoid giant single models.
responses.R2:
Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Settings: StreamingMinRadius ~64 (default), StreamingTargetRadius ~1024 default (lower, e.g. 256-512, for mobile memory), StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic (stream out to save memory), StreamingIntegrityMode = Default or PauseOutsideLoadedArea (pause character if area not loaded). Use Model.ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must arrive whole, Persistent only for few always-needed things (sparingly), PersistentPerPlayer + Player:AddReplicationFocus as needed; use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleporting a player.
Scripts: client code must not assume instances exist: replace direct paths with WaitForChild (with timeout) on non-persistent content, or better CollectionService tags with GetInstanceAddedSignal/RemovedSignal to bind and unbind as content streams in/out; handle nil and instances disappearing (stream out); server scripts are unaffected (server has everything). Use Model LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant imposters. Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleports or spawns. Scripts: client scripts can no longer assume something exists. prompt: Your game autosaves every player's data with SetAsync every 5 seconds. With 80 players you see DataStore queue warnings and sometimes lost saves (queue full, error code 302). Explain the cause and a better design.
answer_key: Requests are throttled by per-server and per-experience budgets that scale with player count; exceeding them queues requests, and a full queue (30 requests) drops them with codes such as 302 for SetAsync
Reduce frequency (autosave every few minutes, staggered), save only changed data, and combine fields into one key rather than many keys
Wrap calls in pcall with retry/backoff, and always save on PlayerRemoving/BindToClose

responses.R1: Each SetAsync is a write request. 80 players every 5 s = ~960 writes/min from one server, far above the per-server write budget (~60 + 40 x players per minute, with the experience-wide 300 + 20 x CCU cap) and the per-key ~6 s write cooldown, so requests queue; when the queue (30) is full further calls fail immediately (301-306 throttle errors, 302 queue full) -> lost saves. Better: keep data cached in memory, mark dirty on change, autosave each player every 2-3 minutes with staggered timers/jitter and only if dirty; save on PlayerRemoving, before teleports, after important purchases, and in BindToClose; use UpdateAsync with session locking and exponential-backoff retries; check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before non-critical writes; or use ProfileStore.
responses.R2:
Cause: 80 players x SetAsync every 5 s = ~960 writes/min, above the write budget (~300 + 20 x CCU per experience per minute since mid-2026; per-server limits are similar ~60 + 10 x players) and above the per-key limit (a key can be written about once every 6 s). Requests queue; when a key's queue fills (30) further requests fail with error 302 (queue full), so saves are dropped; SetAsync also overwrites blindly.
Better design: keep data in a server-side session cache (profile); save with UpdateAsync (session lock) only on a slow autosave interval (~60-120 s, staggered/jittered per player), on PlayerRemoving, on important events (purchases - immediately via receipt flow), and in BindToClose. Skip saves when the data hasn't changed (dirty flag). Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing and back off on errors with retries. Use ProfileStore/ProfileService-style libraries.
responses.R3: Cause: 80 players x every 5 s = 960 writes/min, far above the write budget (about 300 + 20 x CCU per experience, 60 + 10 x players per server historically), and above the per-key limit (writes to the same key roughly once every 6 s). The requests pile up in the 30-slot request queue, then the queue fills and requests fail, and saves are dropped. SetAsync also blindly overwrites, so a failed or out-of-order write can lose data. Better design: keep data in memory (a session cache or profile) and mark it dirty on change. Autosave each player every 60-120 s, staggered with a random per-player offset and jitter, and only if dirty. Save immediately on important events (purchases, trades), debounced. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (parallel, with a deadline). Use UpdateAsync with session locking, pcall plus exponential-backoff retries, and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving. Keep one key per player (combine stats into one table). Use ProfileStore or a similar library. Put leaderboards and ephemeral counters in MemoryStore or OrderedDataStore at low frequency.
responses.R4: 80 players saving every 5 s is about 960 writes per minute. That exceeds the write budget (300 + 20 x CCU, about 1,900/min shared, and the per-key limit allows only about 1 write per 6 s), and the per-server request queues fill up, so requests are throttled or dropped ('queue full', 302) and saves are lost. Repeated SetAsync to the same key also hits the per-key write cooldown. Better design: keep data in memory per session, with a dirty flag. Autosave each player every 60-180 s, staggered with a random offset per player and jitter, skipping clean data. Use UpdateAsync with session locking. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (in parallel), and immediately only on important events like purchases. On failure, retry with exponential backoff, never in a tight loop. Watch DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving, and log the budget. Merge changes into one write per player rather than several keys.
responses.R5: Saving 80 players every 5 s means about 16 writes per second (960 per minute), above the per-server write budget (about 60 + 40 x players per minute) and the per-key write limits/cooldown, and every save happens in synchronized bursts. The 30-request queue fills, saves stall, and they then fail with errors 301-306 (for example 302: SetAsync queue full), so some saves are lost. SetAsync also overwrites blindly, risking rollbacks. Better: keep data in memory (a session-locked profile) and autosave only changed (dirty) profiles about every 60-120 s, with a random offset per player so saves are spread out. Use UpdateAsync with retry and exponential backoff and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType. Save immediately only on important events (purchases, debounced), and on PlayerRemoving and BindToClose. A library such as ProfileStore does this for you.
responses.R6:
Cause: 80 players x 1 save / 5 s = ~960 writes/min, in bursts on the same tick. Even within the experience budget (write 300 + 20 x CCU/min, plus per-server limits ~60 + 40 x players), bursts overflow the DataStore request queue (30 requests per queue); queued calls wait and then fail with queue-full errors (301-306, e.g. 302), so saves are dropped. Blind SetAsync also overwrites newer data and doesn't protect against other servers.
Better design:
- Keep data in a server session cache; mark dirty on change.
- Autosave every 60-180 s, staggered with a random per-player offset, only if dirty.
- Save on PlayerRemoving (releasing the session lock) and in BindToClose (all players in parallel, ~25 s deadline).
- Use UpdateAsync with a session lock instead of SetAsync.
- Check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving; on failure retry with exponential backoff, not instantly (instant retries refill the full queue).
- Optionally use a profile library (ProfileStore) that does all this.
responses.R7: Saving 80 players every 5s is ~960 SetAsync per minute from one server, a large chunk of the experience write budget (300 + 20 x CCU per minute, shared by all servers and Open Cloud; per server 60 + 40 x players), and all fired on the same tick, so the request queue (30 per type) overflows: 302 is the SetAsync queue-full throttle and dropped requests mean lost saves; per-key write rate also caps saves to the same key (roughly once every 6s). Better: keep data in a session cache, mark it dirty on change, autosave every 60-300s per player with staggered/jittered offsets, only if dirty; use UpdateAsync with session locking (or ProfileStore); save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose; retry with exponential backoff and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing; keep profiles small.

prompt: Describe Roblox's Input Action System: its three core instance types, how an action signals a press, and how a menu context is made to take precedence over the default player scripts.
answer_key: Core instances: InputContext (group of actions; Enabled and Priority), InputAction (has a Type such as Bool/Direction1D/2D/3D/ViewportPosition), InputBinding (maps hardware input to an action)
Bool actions fire Pressed and Released; StateChanged fires for all action types
Higher context Priority processes input first; enabling Sink consumes bound KeyCodes and blocks lower-priority contexts
Enabled per project with the Workspace property PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem

responses.R1: Three core instances: InputContext (a group of actions that can be enabled or disabled, with Priority and Sink), InputAction (a semantic action like "Jump" or "Sprint", with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition) and InputBinding (maps a physical input to the action: KeyCode, gamepad buttons, axes, or UIButton for touch). Bindings are children of actions, and actions are children of contexts. Signals: Bool actions fire InputAction.Pressed and Released, and every type fires StateChanged(newState). You can poll InputAction:GetState() each frame for analog values. Precedence: give the menu's InputContext a higher Priority than the default player-scripts/gameplay context, and set Sink = true so the inputs it binds are consumed and not passed to lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens (ctx.Enabled = true) and disable it on close, which hands those keys back to movement or camera. Default player scripts use IAS when Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem is enabled.
responses.R2: Three core instances: InputContext (a group/layer of actions that can be enabled/disabled, with a Priority and Sink), InputAction (the abstract action, with a Type such as Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition), and InputBinding (maps a physical input to the action: KeyCode, gamepad buttons/thumbsticks, or a UIButton for touch). A Bool action signals a press through its Pressed and Released events (and StateChanged with the new value; GetState to poll). Menu precedence: put menu actions in a separate InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player scripts' contexts and Sink = true, and enable it when the menu opens (disable on close), so its bindings consume the input before lower-priority contexts (movement/jump) receive it.
responses.R3:
Three core instances:
- InputContext: groups actions (e.g. Gameplay, Menu); Enabled, Priority, Sink.
- InputAction: an abstract action (Sprint, Jump); Type (Enum.InputActionType: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition...); events Pressed, Released (Bool only), StateChanged; GetState(); Fire() for simulation.
- InputBinding: maps device input to the action - KeyCode (keyboard/gamepad), UIButton (touch GuiButton), modifiers, Scale/composite directions.
Press signaling: a Bool action fires Pressed when any binding becomes active (Released when it ends); StateChanged fires with the new state for every type; poll GetState() for held input.
Menu precedence: put menu actions in a separate InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay/default player-script contexts and Sink = true, so bound inputs are consumed by the menu and not passed to lower-priority contexts (like character movement); enable it when the menu opens (or disable the Gameplay context) and disable it on close. Default player scripts use IAS when Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem is Enabled.
responses.R4: Three core instances. InputContext groups actions and has Enabled, Priority and Sink. InputAction is one logical action with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition. InputBinding maps hardware to the action: KeyCode (keyboard, mouse or gamepad), UIButton for an on-screen touch button, and modifiers or composite directions. They're nested InputContext > InputAction > InputBinding. A Bool action signals a press with InputAction.Pressed and Released, StateChanged(newState) fires when the value changes, and you can poll GetState() (for analog input, poll every frame). Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in their own InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay or default player-script contexts, and enable Sink so inputs it consumes don't reach lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens and disable it on close, or disable the gameplay context. With Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem on, the default character controls also run as InputContexts, so a higher-priority sinking menu context overrides movement and jump.

An action signals through events: Pressed and Released (Bool type), StateChanged (fires on any change, for all types), or polling with action:GetState(). prompt: What is Roblox's CSS-like UI styling system? Name the main instances and explain how styles reach the UI and how a value is shared via tokens.
answer_key: Instances: StyleSheet (rules, tokens, themes), StyleRule (Selector + SetProperties), StyleLink (links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui and its descendants), StyleDerive (inherit another sheet's tokens/themes)
Selectors can match class, tag (CollectionService), name, UI modifiers (e.g. UICorner), GuiState (e.g. Hover), and queries with '@'
Tokens are attributes on a token StyleSheet referenced with a '$' prefix (e.g. '$FrameColor'); themes are sets of tokens; only one StyleSheet applies to a given tree

responses.R1:
Roblox's UI Styling (style sheets) system applies CSS-like rules to GuiObjects.
Instances:
- StyleSheet: container of rules (and token attributes).
- StyleRule: a Selector (class names e.g. ".Primary" from GuiObject tags, instance class e.g. "TextButton", names "#Close", pseudo-state ":hover"/":press" via GuiState, child/descendant combinators, @queries) plus properties set via SetProperty/SetProperties; Priority; rules can nest.
- StyleLink: placed in a ScreenGui/LayerCollector, its StyleSheet property links a sheet to that UI tree (one sheet per tree).
- StyleDerive: lets a sheet inherit rules/tokens from another sheet (base theme -> overrides).
- StyleQuery: conditional rules (MaxSize, PreferredInput etc.) - beta.
How styles reach UI: StyleLink connects the sheet; matching rules apply to the GuiObjects in that tree, re-evaluated when tags/state change; properties set directly in code can conflict, so don't set the same property both ways.
Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (e.g. PrimaryColor = Color3) and reference them in rules as "$PrimaryColor"; swapping/deriving the token sheet re-themes the whole UI (light/dark).
responses.R2: Roblox's UI Styling system is a CSS-like set of instances. StyleSheet holds the rules and tokens. StyleRule has a Selector (class name, .tag, #name, :state like :hover, descendant/child combinators) and property values set via SetProperty/SetProperties, plus a Priority. StyleDerive makes one sheet inherit rules from another (themes, base sheets). StyleLink is placed in a ScreenGui (or other UI root) and points at a StyleSheet, applying it to that UI tree. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect ratio, input type). Styles reach the UI because a StyleLink connects the sheet to a UI tree, and its rules then match GuiObjects by class, tag (CollectionService or the styling tags) or name, the way CSS does. Rule priority and specificity resolve conflicts, and properties set directly on an instance override styles. Tokens: define attributes on a (token) StyleSheet, for example PrimaryColor = Color3, and reference them in rule values as "$PrimaryColor". Swapping or deriving token sheets changes the theme everywhere. The Studio Style Editor is still in beta, and the selector syntax may change.
responses.R3: It's the engine's UI styling system, which works like CSS. A StyleSheet contains StyleRules. Each StyleRule has a Selector (class names like `.Primary` via GuiObject tags, instance class like `TextButton`, `#Name`, pseudo-states like `:hover`/GuiState, `@` queries) and property values (SetProperties). StyleLink, parented under a ScreenGui (or a UI tree), points at a StyleSheet and applies its rules to that tree. StyleDerive lets one sheet inherit from another (a theme base). StyleQuery changes rules by size or input. Tokens: define them as attributes on a token or design StyleSheet (e.g. PrimaryColor = Color3) and reference them in rule properties as "$PrimaryColor". Changing the token updates every rule that uses it, which is good for theming. Don't set the same property both from scripts and from styles.
responses.R4: Roblox UI Styling (Style Editor, beta) applies CSS-like rules to GuiObjects. Instances: StyleSheet (container of rules), StyleRule (a Selector - class name like TextButton, tag/class ".Primary", "#Name", pseudo-states/children - plus properties set via SetProperty/SetProperties), StyleDerive (makes a sheet inherit another, e.g. a token/theme sheet), StyleLink (put under a ScreenGui/UI tree; its StyleSheet property links a sheet so its rules apply to that tree), and StyleQuery for responsive/conditional rules. Styles reach UI by linking via StyleLink and matching selectors against instances (CollectionService tags act as classes). Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (e.g. PrimaryColor) and reference them in rule properties as "$PrimaryColor"; swapping the derived token sheet re-themes every rule using it.
responses.R5: It's Roblox's UI styling system, like CSS for GuiObjects. The instances: StyleSheet is a collection of rules (and also works as a token or theme sheet). StyleRule has a Selector (class name like 'TextButton', a '.tag' from CollectionService, '#Name', states like ':hover', pseudo/child selectors) and properties set with SetProperty or SetProperties, plus Priority. StyleDerive lets a sheet inherit or derive from another sheet. StyleLink connects a StyleSheet to a UI tree: parent it under a ScreenGui (or other root) and point its StyleSheet at the sheet, and its rules then apply to matching descendants. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect or input type, like media queries). How styles reach the UI: StyleLink in the tree, then the sheet's rules match by selector and set properties, with more specific or higher-priority rules winning and explicitly set properties possibly conflicting (don't set the same property from both code and a style). Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (for example Primary = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim), reference them in rules as '$Primary', and share them through StyleDerive. Theming means swapping token sheets with the same names at runtime. The Style Editor is still in beta.
responses.R6: Roblox's UI Styling system (Style Editor) applies CSS-like rules to GuiObjects. Main instances: StyleSheet (a container of rules, also used as a token/theme sheet), StyleRule (has a Selector, e.g. class name, .tag, #Name, state like :hover, and property values via SetProperty/SetProperties; can nest and has Priority), StyleLink (parented under a ScreenGui/LayerCollector or GuiObject with StyleSheet pointing at a sheet, which applies the sheet to that subtree), StyleDerive (lets a sheet inherit rules from another sheet), and StyleQuery (conditional rules by size/input). Styles reach UI when a StyleLink connects the sheet to the UI tree and selectors match instances (by ClassName, tags via CollectionService-style tags, or name); matched properties override defaults. Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (e.g. PrimaryColor), derive it into your sheet, and reference them in rule values as "$PrimaryColor"; swapping the token sheet (StyleDerive) changes themes everywhere.
responses.R7:
Roblox's engine UI styling system (CSS-like, StyleSheets):
- StyleSheet: container of rules (usually in ReplicatedStorage).
- StyleRule: has a Selector (class name like "TextButton", tag ".PrimaryButton" via CollectionService tags, "#Name", pseudo-states like ":hover", "::"-phantom modifiers e.g. UICorner, nested child rules) and property overrides set with StyleRule:SetProperty / SetProperties; Priority resolves conflicts.
- StyleLink: placed in a ScreenGui (or other UI root) with StyleLink.StyleSheet = the sheet; that's how styles reach that UI tree - matching descendants get the properties applied automatically and live-update.
- StyleDerive: makes a sheet inherit rules from another (base design system -> theme).
- StyleQuery (conditional, e.g. screen size / preferred input).
Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (tokens:SetAttribute("Primary", Color3.fromRGB(...))) and reference them in rules as "$Primary"; derive the main sheet from the token sheet. Swapping the token sheet (e.g. dark/light theme with same attribute names) re-themes everything. Don't also set those properties in scripts (conflicts). Studio has a Style Editor (beta).

prompt: In late 2025 / early 2026 Roblox began requiring age checks for chat. What method does the check use, what age groups are used, and how does it restrict who can chat with whom?
answer_key: Facial age estimation via the app camera (ID verification as an alternative for older users); under-9 users also need parental approval
Chat is limited to users in the same or similar (adjacent) age groups, e.g. a 13-15 user can chat with those 15 or younger but not the 16+ groups
Rollout began in select regions in December 2025 and extended worldwide where chat is available in January 2026

responses.R1: The method is facial age estimation (a selfie video through Roblox's vendor, processed then deleted), with optional ID verification for 13+. It was announced Nov 2025, tested Dec 2025 in Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands, and made global in Jan 2026; chat requires a completed age check. Age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20, 21+. Restriction: users can chat only with their own and adjacent (similar) age groups, under-9s have chat off by default, and trusted connections (verified friends) can widen this. Developers don't see ages: use TextChatService:GetChatGroupsAsync, CanUsersChatAsync and CanUsersDirectChatAsync before creating private channels, and design for players who can't chat with each other.
responses.R2: Roblox requires an age check to access chat, rolled out from late 2025 and globally in early 2026. It uses facial age estimation through the Roblox app, with a camera selfie processed by a vendor (Persona), and ID verification or parental controls can correct an estimate. Age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+. Restriction: by default, users can chat only with their own age group and the adjacent groups (for example, 13-15 with 9-12 and 16-17), which keeps minors and adults apart (under-16s can't chat with adults). Under-9s need parental consent for chat. Trusted Connections (13+, verified real-world contacts) can chat beyond the bands. Unchecked users can't use chat. Messages from users you can't chat with are hidden from you.
